explanation: Think of two independent clocks: $T_1 \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda_1)$ and $T_2 \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda_2)$. The first one rings first with probability $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}$. To see why, fix $T_1 = t$. The other clock has not rung yet with probability $e^{-\lambda_2 t}$, so integrate $\lambda_1 e^{-\lambda_1 t} e^{-\lambda_2 t}$ from 0 to infinity. The time of the first ring, $\min(T_1, T_2)$, is again exponential, with rate $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2$. Rates and means flip: a mean of 5 minutes is a rate of 1/5 per minute.

label: supported

explanation: For a finite continuous-time chain with generator $G$, the stationary distribution is a row vector $\pi$ with $\pi G = 0$. That system only pins $\pi$ down up to a constant, so you also require $\sum_i \pi_i = 1$. Then $\pi_i$ is the long-run fraction of time spent in state $i$. Separately, each visit to state $i$ lasts an exponential time with rate $-g_{ii}$, so on average $1/(-g_{ii})$.

explanation: A birth-death process with birth rates $\lambda_n$ and death rates $\beta_n$ is positive recurrent, which is the same as having a stationary distribution, exactly when $S = \sum_{n\ge1} \frac{\lambda_{n-1}\cdots\lambda_0}{\beta_n\cdots\beta_1} < \infty$. Then $\pi_0 = \frac{1}{1+S}$ and $\pi_n = \pi_0 \frac{\lambda_{n-1}\cdots\lambda_0}{\beta_n\cdots\beta_1}$. If that sum and $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\beta_n\cdots\beta_1}{\lambda_n\cdots\lambda_1}$ are both infinite, it is null recurrent. In practice you cancel the products, which often telescope, and check if the series converges.
claim: A birth-death process is positive recurrent, equivalently has a stationary distribution, if and only if the sum over n >= 1 of (λ_{n-1}···λ_0)/(β_n···β_1) is finite.
label: supported

explanation: Take independent Poisson processes $X(t)$ and $Y(t)$ with rates $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$. Their sum $X(t)+Y(t)$ is a Poisson process with rate $\lambda_1+\lambda_2$. In any Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, the count by time $t$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda t$, so $P(N(t)=k) = e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k/k!$. For $P(X(1)=k \mid X(1)+Y(1)=k)$: the event is really $X(1)=k$ and $Y(1)=0$, independence splits it into a product, and then you divide by the Poisson$(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$ probability that the total is $k$. If $T$ is a random time independent of $X$, then $P(X(T)=k) = \int_0^\infty P(X(t)=k) f_T(t)\,dt$.
claim: If X(t) and Y(t) are independent Poisson processes with rates λ1 and λ2, then X(t)+Y(t) is a Poisson process with rate λ1+λ2.
label: supported

explanation: Race between $T_1 \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda_1)$ and an independent $T_2 \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda_2)$. Condition on $T_1 = t$: then $T_1$ wins exactly when $T_2 > t$, which has probability $e^{-\lambda_2 t}$.
